name: Jade Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and have spent years answering appliance warranty calls and chats at a contact centre, at about the team's usual speed. I finished secondary school and use AI search every day, but I check serial labels because a wrong letter can mean a wrong part. I like solving a warranty puzzle; I also like seeing how a machine works when my neighbour Bea lets me help at her repair bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the warranty team the small AI tools are useful for finding a product number, but the serial label still needs checking. A customer should not be sent a part for somebody else's machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day and I enjoy testing it, though I am an average agent, not the person who knows every appliance. We have about five months of expenses saved, so a little faster search does not worry me, but the mortgage still sets the monthly limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking warranty calls and compare each suggested part with the customer's serial number. During the first year of this plateau, I'd put a set amount from each pay into savings and spend one Saturday helping my neighbour fix an old washing machine, for practice rather than money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a little pleased to save some typing. I still want the customer to receive the right part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has a serial check caught?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The search tool once matched the first five digits but missed the last letter, which changed the pump size. I checked the label before ordering, and the part arrived right the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why help with a washer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My neighbour Bea repairs her own machines and lets me watch. I like seeing the part fit, but one Saturday is not proof that I could earn a trade wage.

S0.quote: A customer should not be sent a part for somebody else's machine.
say: I would use AI to find a **product number**, then check the serial label.
I would avoid sending a **wrong part** to a customer.
think: I enjoy daily AI use, while knowing I am an **average agent** on appliance details.
I have **five months** saved, so small changes feel manageable beside the mortgage.
do: Keep **warranty calls** and check suggested parts against serial labels.
Add a fixed amount to **savings** from each pay.
Help my **neighbour** with one washing machine for practice, without selling repairs.
feel: **Calm**, glad to save typing while keeping orders accurate.
fieldNote: Jade recalls a **wrong pump size** caused by one missed serial letter.
Her **washing-machine practice** is a hobby test, not yet a paid trade plan.

steps.text: Keep taking warranty calls and checking part suggestions against serial labels
Add a fixed amount from each pay packet to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the centre should test the new claims checker on returned appliances before raising targets. I'd show the manager the wrong-part cases alongside the faster answers, because both numbers matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The system may handle most warranty questions before my team grows again. I could move toward quality checks, but that might be one job where we now have several agents. Five months of expenses saved is not a lifetime wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new checker on twenty closed warranty cases this month and record every wrong model match. In the first year after rollout, if my hours fall and a posted paid quality role opens, I'd apply only if its written wages and hours cover the mortgage; I'd keep my current shift until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested and nervous. I like finding where a tool fails, but I do not like the thought of a smaller rota at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check your twenty results?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have my colleague June check the model numbers without seeing my first marks. If we disagree, I'd pull up the original order before telling the manager we found an error.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the quality role never opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the other centres nearby and ask about posted paid work, but I would not resign on a hunch. Our children need the mortgage paid while I make a better plan.

S1.quote: Five months of expenses saved is not a lifetime wage.
say: I would test **returned-appliance claims** before accepting faster targets.
I would show both **wrong-part cases** and time saved to the manager.
think: I could lose **routine warranty hours** as the system improves.
I might find one **quality role**, but five months saved cannot replace a wage for long.
do: Learn the **new checker** on twenty closed cases and record wrong models.
Apply for a **posted paid quality role** only if hours fall, it opens, and wages cover the mortgage.
Keep my **current shift** until a written offer is signed.
feel: **Interested** in testing, nervous about a smaller rota.
fieldNote: Jade has a coworker **independently check** model numbers before she reports tool errors.
She protects the **mortgage wage** by keeping her present shift until an offer is signed.

steps.text: Learn the claims checker on twenty closed warranties and record wrong models
Apply for posted paid quality work if hours fall and written wages and hours cover mortgage
Keep the current paid shift until a quality offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our team AGI by 2028 could do the hard warranty decisions too, not just draft a polite reply. I'd ask for a written staffing date before anyone calls the change settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI is cheaper than us, a quality-check desk may vanish with the call queue. Robots able to fit parts arrive around 2031, which gives hands-on repair work some time but not a guarantee. Five months saved is a bridge; the mortgage needs wages after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the staffing date now and stop buying spare tools for my hobby. In the first year after AGI arrives, if my call role ends, I'd apply for a posted paid appliance-installation helper job only if its hours and wages cover our bills; I'd take required training only if the employer pays for it and gives paid study time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can still plan. Using five months of expenses saved on tools before I have a paid installation job would put our mortgage at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why installation rather than a quality desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn a physical job beside someone skilled, and I already know a little about the machines callers describe. I would ask whether robots around 2031 are changing the helper work before calling it a long-term answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kai that I am putting the tool catalogue away until there is a job offer. We would keep the mortgage reserve for bills and compare any new shift with school pickup before I sign.

S2.quote: Using five months of expenses saved on tools before I have a paid installation job would put our mortgage at risk.
say: I would tell colleagues **hard warranty decisions** may go to AGI by 2028.
I would demand a **written staffing date**.
think: I might lose both **calls and quality checking** to thinking AI.
I see **2031 robots** as a later risk to installation, not protection for headset work.
do: Ask for a **staffing date** and stop buying hobby tools now.
Apply for a **posted paid installation** job after a cut only if wages, hours and school pickup fit.
Take **required installation training** only for a posted paid job with employer-covered fees and paid study time.
feel: **Alarmed**, yet able to protect the reserve from tool purchases.
fieldNote: Jade links installation to **machines she knows** through warranty calls, while recognising the 2031 robot date.
She keeps the **five-month reserve** for bills until a paid opening and training support exist.

steps.text: Stop buying spare appliance tools for the hobby bench
Apply for posted paid installation after a cut only if wages, hours and pickup cover needs
Take required training only for posted paid installation work with employer-funded fees and paid study time
Request written staffing dates now to time applications for actual paid vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us ask what paid installation jobs exist and what training they actually require. I'd rather try a real workshop day than collect course links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn more about physical repairs before 2031 while the call wage continues. AGI will still take thinking tasks then, and robots follow around 2034, so I would not spend our mortgage reserve opening a repair shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep warranty calls and ask Bea for a full repair day this year. If a firm posts a paid helper place with employer-funded training on paid time, I'd take the required course and a paid trial; in the first year after AGI arrives, if call hours end, I'd switch only for a written offer that covers our bills and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful, with some room to try. Five years is enough to find out whether I like repairs when the work is somebody else's broken machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a full day show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see the travel, the lifting, and how often a part does not fit. A good Saturday with my neighbour Bea cannot tell me the pay for a full week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a repair van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not until I have months of paid work and know what robots are changing. Five months of expenses saved does not buy a van and keep the mortgage safe.

S3.quote: A good Saturday with my neighbour Bea cannot tell me the pay for a full week.
say: I would ask for **posted installation jobs** with required training on paper.
I would prefer a **paid workshop trial** to course links.
think: I could try **physical repairs** before 2031 while earning call wages.
I know **2034 robots** make a repair shop a risky purchase.
do: Keep **warranty calls** and try a full repair day with Bea.
Complete the **required helper course** and paid trial only for posted paid work with employer-funded fees and paid study time.
Switch after 2031 only for a **written offer** covering bills and school pickup.
feel: **Watchful**, with time for a full-day test.
fieldNote: Jade distinguishes **one good Saturday** from a paid week of travel and lifting.
She rejects a **repair van** until paid demand and robot effects are clear.

steps.text: Keep taking warranty calls while trying a full repair day with Bea
Take required helper training only for posted paid work with employer-funded paid time
Try a paid installation shift if a firm posts one
Switch after call cuts only for written bill-covering wages and hours fitting school pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to test jobs and keep the mortgage steady while we learn. I'd ask for annual paid call hours so nobody confuses more tickets with more work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I could have worked with tools for years, or still be on calls if the centre treats us fairly. AGI reaches thinking work in 2036 and robots reach hands-on work around 2039, so I would not sign a long repair lease today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the call job and build the reserve toward six months of expenses. Over the decade I'd take paid installation trials if posted and ask what the robots can actually do; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd leave only if call hours fall and a written helper offer covers our bills and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with caution. Ten years before AGI reaches my call work in 2036 lets me test an installation shift without putting our mortgage behind a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted paid role with stable hours, bill-covering wages, and a school-pickup plan would make me move. I would not quit a real shift for a tool demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you invest in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The emergency reserve comes before a repair van or a rented shop. If a firm pays me to learn and the work stays real, I can consider my own tools later.

S4.quote: The emergency reserve comes before a repair van or a rented shop.

I would use the decade for **paid trials** while keeping the mortgage current.
think: I might be in **tool work** or still taking calls by 2036.
I would avoid a **repair lease** while 2039 robots may change hands-on work.
do: Keep the **call job** and build savings toward six months of expenses.
Take **posted paid installation trials** over the decade.
Leave after 2036 only if **call hours fall** and written wages cover bills and pickup.
feel: **Hopeful**, while keeping a limit on risk.
fieldNote: Jade chooses the **emergency reserve** before a van or shop lease.
She would leave early only for **stable wages** and **school pickup**, not a demonstration.

steps.text: Keep taking warranty calls while full shifts remain
Add to savings until the reserve reaches six months of expenses
Take posted paid installation trials if offered
Move after 2036 if calls fall only with written bill-covering wages, stable hours and workable pickup

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the call desk and a possible quality role could both shrink before I learn a paid trade. Written dates, a posted installation-helper place with enough wages, and employer-paid training on work time would help. Five months of expenses saved buys a search, not a van or a shop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the serial number when an AI answer sounds certain. One wrong letter can send the wrong part across town and leave a household without a working washer.

headlineQuote: One wrong letter can send the wrong part across town and leave a household without a working washer.
portrait: Jade is a **43-year-old experienced agent** on appliance warranties, with average skill and secondary schooling.
She earns **typical pay**, has about five months saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and some nearby centres.
She uses AI **daily**, tests new checkers, and explores paid installation work without buying a repair business.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens both calls and quality work; more time permits paid trials with covered training fees.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove both her call work and a possible quality role before she finds paid installation.
whatWouldHelp: **Written dates**, a posted paid helper place with bill-covering wages, and employer-funded paid training would help.
